items.title: Building This Portfolio: 7 Templates, 5 Colors, 3 Languages
items.excerpt: One JSON, many faces — how this site renders 7 templates from a single content source.
items.content:
This portfolio is not a single design — it is a small engine that renders **7 templates**, each switchable in one click. Let me break down how it works.

## One JSON, Many Faces

Every template (minimal, playful, classic, brutalist, fashion, pastel, glass) reads from the same `src/data/{lang}.json`. The content never changes — only the presentation does.

The result: I can swap my entire site's look without touching a single word of content.

## The Switching Logic

A `TemplateProvider` holds the current template in state and persists it to the URL via `UrlStateSync`, so the chosen template survives a refresh and is shareable as a link.

```
?template=glass&scheme=ocean&lang=en
```

## What I Learned

- Data-driven UI makes redesigns trivial.
- URL state is the cheapest persistence layer there is.
- Cute animations (float, wiggle, pop) add personality with very little code.

> Build systems, not one-off pages.

items.title: Designing a Color Scheme System That Feels Yours
items.excerpt: Five palettes, dark & light, zero flash — the story behind the theme engine.
items.content:
Color is a feature, not decoration. I wanted every visitor to be able to make the site feel like their own, so I built a color scheme system with five palettes — mauve, pastel, ocean, forest, and sunset.

## How It Works

Each palette defines CSS variables for background, foreground, accent, accent-2, muted, card, and border. The `@theme inline` block in Tailwind v4 maps those variables to utility classes like `bg-background` and `text-accent`.

```
scheme-ocean + .dark  =>  deep blue, cyan accents
scheme-pastel + .dark =>  soft pink, lavender
```

## No Flash of Wrong Theme

An inline script in `<head>` reads `localStorage` before first paint, so the correct theme applies before the page renders — no flicker.

## Dark & Light

Each palette ships with both variants. Toggling is instant and saved.

> Choose your own adventure.

items.title: Deploying a Next.js Static Site to GitHub Pages
items.excerpt: The exact recipe for free hosting with Next.js static export and GitHub Actions.
items.content:
This site runs on Next.js with `output: 'export'` and is hosted for free on GitHub Pages. Here is the exact recipe.

## 1. Configure Static Export

In `next.config.ts`:

```
output: "export",
images: { unoptimized: true },
```

Static exports mean no server, which is perfect for GitHub Pages.

## 2. Add a Workflow

A small GitHub Actions workflow builds the site on every push to `main` and publishes the `out/` folder to the `gh-pages` branch.

## 3. Don't Forget .nojekyll

GitHub Pages runs Jekyll by default. Adding a `.nojekyll` file ensures raw static files are served correctly.

## Result

Push to `main` → site is live in under a minute. Zero hosting cost, zero server maintenance.

> Free hosting, full control.
